📚 Today you learned

Stop Trigger Logic — Intraday Touch vs. Closing Price

A stop order — plain or stop-limit — triggers the instant the stock trades at or through your stop price, on any tick during the session. It does not wait for the close, and it does not care whether the stock recovers five minutes later. That's exactly today's GOOG question: if Friday's reported $330.71 low is accurate, your $333.90 plain STOP would have fired right there, mid-session — regardless of the fact that GOOG apparently closed back up near $335.45. In forex you're used to watching the candle close before trusting a level break; single-name equity stops don't grant that grace period intraday. The practical lesson: once a stop is live, treat every reported intraday low as a potential trigger event worth checking, not just the day's close — because by the time you see the close, the order may already be filled.

Also today: Wick vs. body — the intraday low (the "wick") is where stops and liquidity get tested; the close (the "body") is just where the auction happened to land, and the two can tell very different stories on the same candle.
